The Chapter of the Cat and Rat

p.n: The King Asks about Escaping Enemies

body.p:
“I have heard this parable,” said the King to the Philosopher. “Present to me the parable of the man
whose enemies are going to vanquish him-how can he get rid of them

p.n: The Philosopher Responds that Emotions Change

body.p:
The Philosopher
said: “He who has been vanquished by his enemies and fallen victim to them should seek the friendship
of one of the enemies, make him a dear friend, and enter into a pact with him, so as he can defeat, with his aid], the rest of his enemies. For
a friend is not always a friend nor an enemy always an enemy: if a friend sees
in his friend that which he abhors, he turns to enmity, and if the enemy sees profit to be had from his enemy,
he doesn’t hold on to his enmity; rather, he changes to friendship and loyalty.

The man of knowledge
proceeds, when compelled, to befriend his enemies. And he who doesn’t know looses his way
of things; and he recognizes neither motive nor direction until he perishes in blindness.

p.n: The Parable of the Cat and Rat Is Invoked

body.p:
A example of this is the parable of
the cat and the rat, who escaped from a trap with either one doing the other a favor.

p.n: The King Requests the Full Parable
